content: Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain can impair mental and physical abilities necessary for performing potentially hazardous tasks, such as driving or operating machinery. This impairment may be exacerbated when combined with other central nervous system depressants, including alcohol, sedatives, hypnotics (e.g., barbiturates), narcotics, general anesthetics, tricyclic antidepressants, and tranquilizers. Therefore, these substances should either be avoided or used in reduced doses when Promethazine HCl is administered. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain has the potential to cause life-threatening respiratory depression. Its use should be avoided in patients with compromised respiratory function, such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or sleep apnea. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain may lower the seizure threshold, increasing the risk of seizures. It should be used cautiously in individuals with seizure disorders or those taking medications, such as narcotics or local anesthetics, that may also affect seizure thresholds. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain should be used with caution in patients with bone marrow depression, as it has been associated with leukopenia and agranulocytosis, particularly when used in combination with other marrow-toxic agents. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS), a potentially fatal condition, has been reported with the use of Promethazine HCl, either alone or in combination with antipsychotic drugs. Diagnosing NMS can be challenging, as it requires distinguishing it from other conditions with similar presentations, such as severe medical illnesses (e.g., pneumonia or systemic infections), untreated or inadequately treated extrapyramidal symptoms, central anticholinergic toxicity, heat stroke, drug fever, or primary central nervous system pathology. Management of NMS involves the immediate discontinuation of Promethazine HCl, antipsychotic drugs, and any other non-essential medications. Intensive symptomatic treatment and medical monitoring are required, along with addressing any concurrent serious medical conditions. There is no universally agreed-upon pharmacological treatment for uncomplicated NMS. Recurrences of NMS have been reported with phenothiazines. Therefore, reintroducing Promethazine HCl should be approached with caution. Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain is contraindicated in pediatric patients under two years of age due to the risk of fatal respiratory depression. In children aged two years and older, caution is advised because respiratory depression and apnea, sometimes resulting in death, have been associated with Promethazine products. These risks are not necessarily mitigated by weight-based dosing. Co-administration with other respiratory depressants increases the risk of respiratory depression and death in pediatric patients. The use of antiemetics, including Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain, is not recommended for treating uncomplicated vomiting in pediatric patients. Their use should be limited to cases of prolonged vomiting with a known cause. Extrapyramidal symptoms caused by Promethazine HCl may mimic central nervous system signs of undiagnosed primary diseases, such as encephalopathy or Reye’s syndrome. Promethazine HCl should be avoided in pediatric patients with symptoms suggestive of Reye’s syndrome or other hepatic conditions. Excessive doses of antihistamines, including Promethazine HCl Syrup Plain, can cause sudden death in pediatric patients. Hallucinations and convulsions have been reported with both therapeutic and excessive doses of Promethazine HCl in children. Pediatric patients who are acutely ill and dehydrated are at increased risk of developing dystonic reactions when treated with Promethazine HCl. The use of Promethazine HCl has been associated with cases of cholestatic jaundice.
